column4: Scheduler sessions are not closed when scoring throws
column5: When an ML prediction job starts, it opens a working session with KenyaEMR. If the job fails unexpectedly, that session may remain open instead of being cleaned up.
column8: Each task calls Context.openSession(), runs generation, and calls Context.closeSession() without a finally block.
column9: An unchecked failure can leave an OpenMRS/Hibernate session bound to the scheduler thread, retaining its persistence context and database resources across later executions.
column10: Wrap task execution in try/finally and close only the session opened by the task
column11: add a test that forces generation to throw and asserts cleanup.

column4: Remote IIT responses are not closed
column5: When the ML module sends information to the remote IIT prediction service, some communication channels may remain open after errors.
column8: Both paths execute an OkHttp call into a Response local variable without try-with-resources
column9: successful body.string() consumes a body but error and early-return paths do not guarantee Response.close().
column10: Repeated scoring can strand response bodies/connections, reduce connection-pool availability, and increase native/socket resource use.
column11: Use try (Response response = client.newCall(request).execute()) in every path and avoid returning before the block closes.

column4: IIT local scoring performs seven sequential SQL calls per patient
column5: To calculate one patient's IIT risk score, the module can make seven separate database calls for visits, pharmacy, demographics, labs, ART, ETL status, CD4, etc.
column7: Every local patient score separately executes visits, pharmacy, demographics, lab, ART, last-ETL-update, and CD4 stored procedures; batch generation invokes this in its patient loop at MLDataExchange.java:733-752.
column8: Runtime and database load grow roughly with 7 x patient count
column9: repeated facility-wide runs can saturate the DB and hold scheduler transactions for a long time.
column10: Bulk-fetch features for a bounded patient batch, cache the facility-wide ETL timestamp once per run, consolidate queries where practical, and measure query plans/latency.

column4: Facility-wide jobs materialize all Patient entities and process them in one session
column5: Facility-wide prediction jobs can load the whole eligible patient population into memory and process them in one long session.
column10: Eligibility queries return full result lists, convert every id to a Patient entity, store all Patients in another list, and then score/save them under one scheduler session; no periodic session flush/clear is present.
column11: Large facilities can retain Patient graphs, scores, query results, and dirty entities until job completion, causing long GC pauses or OutOfMemoryError even without a permanent static leak.
column12: Page only patient IDs, load/process a small chunk in a transaction, flush and clear the Hibernate session between chunks, and discard each page before fetching the next.

column4: Dashboard summaries use full patient enumeration plus N+1 queries
column5: To build dashboard summaries, the system first gets the patients and then goes back to the database again and again for each patient.
column8: Both IIT and RTC summaries first list distinct patients and then call getPatientPrograms plus a latest-risk-score query for each patient.
column9: Dashboard latency and database traffic increase linearly with cohort size and can become thousands of queries per page load.
column10: Replace the loop with one grouped/conditional aggregate query restricted to active HIV patients and each patient's latest score

column4: DAO loads the entire risk-score table as entities
column5: Some functions retrieve the complete ML risk-score table, including historical predictions, instead of retrieving only what's needed.
column8: getAllPatients() calls criteria.list() for every PatientRiskScore and builds a second HashSet
column9: getAllPatientRiskScore() also returns the whole entity table without paging.
column10: Risk-score history growth directly raises heap use, hydration cost, and GC pressure; callers can accidentally exhaust heap.
column11: Query distinct patient IDs directly with status predicates, add pagination to history APIs, and remove or tightly restrict the unbounded get-all method.

column4: PMML ZIP streams are never closed
column5: When KenyaEMR loads the actual prediction model, some file resources aren't consistently closed afterwards.
column8: Model initialization opens classpath InputStream, BufferedInputStream, and ZipInputStream objects without try-with-resources.
column9: Normally this leaks only during service initialization, but failed or concurrent initialization attempts can accumulate ZIP/file resources and temporary parsing allocations.
column10: Open the classpath stream and ZipInputStream in try-with-resources, validate null resources, and publish the evaluator only after a successful build.

column5: If several requests arrive when the ML model hasn't initialized yet, multiple requests could all try to load the large model simultaneously.
column8: The shared evaluator field is neither volatile nor guarded
column9: concurrent first requests can all observe null and build the large PMML model independently.
column10: Startup traffic can cause duplicate model parsing, transient heap spikes, leaked streams, and unsafe publication of the evaluator.
column11: Initialize through Spring lifecycle/eager singleton construction or use properly synchronized safe publication
column12: load exactly once and fail startup clearly if invalid.

column4: Facility matrix files are read and parsed repeatedly
column5: Some reference/configuration files used by the ML model are repeatedly opened and parsed instead of being loaded once and reused.
column10: Threshold/profile calls repeatedly open bundled JSON, deserialize the complete array, sometimes stringify it, and parse it again; their InputStreams are not closed.
column11: Every scoring request adds avoidable classpath I/O, full-array allocation, CPU work, and short-lived heap pressure; unclosed streams add a resource-leak risk.
column12: Parse each immutable matrix once at module startup into an MFL-code lookup map, reuse it for profiles and thresholds, and close initialization streams with try-with-resources.

column4: A new OkHttpClient is constructed for individual remote scores
column5: For some remote predictions, the system creates a new communication client every time rather than reusing one.
column9: Remote scoring paths construct new OkHttpClient instances instead of sharing a configured singleton.
column10: Per-patient batch calls lose effective connection-pool/thread-pool reuse and create excess objects, TLS handshakes, threads, and latency.
column11: Inject one module-scoped OkHttpClient with bounded dispatcher/connection-pool settings and explicit connect/read/call timeouts.

column4: Debug mode is hard-coded on and emits/stores large per-patient details
column5: The ML module is configured to record large amounts of detailed information for every patient prediction, including full payload information.
column12: local scoring logs many feature values and payloads and saves the complete payload into PatientRiskScore.
column13: Facility batches generate heavy synchronous console I/O, large logs, sensitive-data exposure, database growth, larger entity hydration, and higher heap/GC load.
column14: Default debug off, use parameterized logger calls with levels/rate limits, never log full clinical payloads, and store diagnostic payloads only behind a time-limited opt-in with retention cleanup.

column4: HTTP request bodies are accumulated with repeated String concatenation
column5: Incoming information is repeatedly joined together piece by piece in memory without a clear size limit.
column8: fetchRequestBody reads until EOF and repeatedly appends each line to an immutable String without enforcing a maximum body size.
column9: Large requests cause quadratic copying and can create a request-scoped memory-exhaustion/GC hotspot.
column10: Use a size-limited StringBuilder or framework JSON binding and configure an application/server request-size limit.

column4: Date-bounded DAO method ignores both date arguments
column5: One function asks for risk scores between certain dates, but the code ignores the dates and retrieves all historical scores for that patient.
column7: getPatientRiskScoreByPatient(patient, onOrBefore, onOrAfter) applies only the patient restriction and returns every historical score.
column8: Callers expecting a bounded window receive and hydrate excessive history as the table grows, increasing response time and memory use.
column9: Add evaluationDate <= onOrBefore and >= onOrAfter restrictions when supplied, order deliberately, and test boundary behavior.

column4: URLConnection calls have no explicit connect/read timeouts
column5: Some communication with OAuth/DWH services doesn't have a clear “stop waiting after X seconds” rule.
column9: OAuth and DWH requests open HttpsURLConnection instances but do not configure connectTimeout or readTimeout.
column10: A stalled remote service can pin the scheduler/request thread and its OpenMRS session, transaction, and object graph indefinitely.
column11: Set finite connect/read timeouts from validated configuration, add bounded retries with backoff, and expose timeout/failure metrics.

column4: Eligibility SQL uses broad aggregation and NOT IN subqueries
column5: Finding which patients qualify for prediction involves large joins and filtering across ETL tables.
column8: The full-facility eligibility statements join and aggregate multiple ETL tables and use patient_id NOT IN subqueries before materializing all results.
column9: On large ETL tables or missing indexes these queries can scan/sort substantial data, create temporary tables, and delay every batch run.
column10: Capture EXPLAIN ANALYZE on representative production-sized data
column11: prefer NOT EXISTS/anti-join where plans improve and ensure indexes cover patient_id plus visit/evaluation dates.
